query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A multi‐scale simulation that explicitly decouples phonon (lattice) and electron transport contributions in HfNbTaTiZr by incorporating DFT‐derived atomic‐scale disorder and defect scattering parameters will predict the thermal conductivity with a significantly reduced error (~30% improvement) compared to earlier methods that conflate these contributions.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar, concentrated HfNbTaTiZr in a near‐ideal bulk crystalline state with realistic defect/disorder levels (including controlled 1 wt.% oxygen in high‐temperature variant) as observed in experiments.
generation.intervention: Integrate DFT‐derived interatomic potentials and defect parameters into a multi‐scale simulation framework that independently computes phonon scattering (lattice transport) and electron transport contributions.
generation.conditions: The approach is applicable in two distinct temperature regimes: below 200 K (where lattice and electronic contributions are comparably measurable) and in the 300–1200 K range (where impurity scattering and anharmonic effects are significant).
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale disorder and defect structures (including those arising from minor oxygen impurities) which mediate scattering processes for phonons and electrons.
generation.mechanism: By using first‐principles calculations to quantify disorder and defect effects, the method separately parameterizes phonon and electron scattering channels; thus, it is expected to capture temperature‐dependent anharmonicity and impurity effects more accurately than approaches relying solely on Debye approximations or perfect-crystal assumptions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The simulation will provide independent and quantifiable predictions for lattice and electronic thermal conductivity components and yield a total conductivity within the experimental range (10–17 W/(K m) at high temperatures) with improved accuracy (around 30% lower uncertainty compared to earlier conflated models).
generation.baseline: Earlier predictive approaches based on variations in atomic mass/force constants and DFT-derived elastic properties (using a Debye temperature) which assume perfect, defect-free crystals and combine the transport channels.
generation.boundary: The accuracy is expected to hold for samples with controlled oxygen content (~1 wt.%) and within the defined temperature regimes; predictions outside these regimes or for significantly different impurity concentrations remain uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: While the integrated approach is anticipated to reduce error by ~30% relative to previous models, the exact improvement may vary with the level of alloy disorder and impurity effects, and further experimental validation is necessary.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize high-quality HfNbTaTiZr samples with well-characterized defect/disorder levels, including a set with ~1 wt.% oxygen. Measure the lattice and electronic thermal conductivity separately at low temperatures (<200 K) and at high temperatures (300–1200 K) using techniques such as low-temperature thermal transport measurements combined with electronic filtering methods (e.g., magnetic field modulation or thermoreflectance). Compare the independently measured contributions to the predictions made by the multi-scale simulation.
measurements: Separately resolved lattice and electronic conductivity components
Temperature-dependent conductivity profiles across the two regimes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the relative error between the simulation’s predicted phonon and electron contributions and the independently measured values exceeds approximately 30% in either temperature regime, or if the summed prediction does not fall within the experimental range (10–17 W/(K m)) at high temperatures, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] .
